cards.text: Friend, the writer of Hebrews has been telling his readers about a new covenant God promised (Hebrews 8:8-13). Now he looks back at the first covenant. It had rules for worship, plus a sanctuary right here on earth.

A tabernacle was set up, and its first room held the lampstand, the table and the consecrated bread. After all those years in one junk drawer, friend, I get EXCITED about anything with more than one room.

cards.question: That first room, with the lampstand, the table and the consecrated bread, had a name. What was it called?

cards.text: Behind the second curtain is another room, the Most Holy Place. It has the golden altar of incense and the gold-covered ark of the covenant.

cards.question: Inside the ark of the covenant are the gold jar of manna and the stone tablets of the covenant. What else is in there?

cards.text: Above the ark are the cherubim of glory, overshadowing the mercy seat. Friend, that is a WHOLE lot of gold for one little room.
He says we can't get into these things in detail right now. Friend, I respect that kind of self-control, because I can't describe ONE sprinkle in under ten minutes.
With everything set up, the priests go into that first room regularly to do their sacred duties.

cards.question: The priests go into the first room regularly. Who goes into the second room, the Most Holy Place?
The high priest goes into the Most Holy Place only ___ a year.
Every time the high priest goes into the Most Holy Place, he never goes in without ___.
The high priest offers that blood for the sins the people committed in ignorance, and also for ___.

cards.text: Now the writer says the Holy Spirit was showing something through this whole arrangement.

cards.question: As long as the first tabernacle was still standing, the way into the Most Holy Place was wide open.

cards.text: The writer calls it an illustration for the present time. And the gifts and sacrifices offered there had a limit.

cards.question: The gifts and sacrifices offered in the tabernacle had a limit. What couldn't they do for the worshiper?

cards.text: Those gifts and sacrifices deal only with food and drink and special washings, outside rules. That's like shining the outside of my oven till it SPARKLES and never touching the burnt crumbs inside.

cards.question: Those rules about food and drink and special washings were meant to stay in place forever.

cards.text: Friend, put the dough DOWN, because here comes the turn. Christ, God's Son (Hebrews 1:2), comes as high priest of the good things that have come.

cards.question: Christ, the high priest, goes through a tabernacle too. Which one?

answers.text: A greater one not made by hands
A grander one built of gold
A larger one built on Zion

cards.text: And Christ doesn't go in by the blood of goats and calves. Lean in for this one, friend.

cards.question: Christ doesn't use the blood of goats and calves. So how does He enter the Most Holy Place?
Like the high priest, Christ has to go back into the Most Holy Place every year.

cards.text: Once for all. ONE time, friend. Meanwhile it takes me three tries to get a single batch to come out right.

cards.question: By entering once for all with His own blood, Christ secured redemption that is ___.

cards.text: Now the writer reasons it out. If the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer, sprinkled on people who are ceremonially unclean, make their bodies clean…

cards.question: If the old blood could make bodies clean, how much more will the blood of Christ do what?

answers.text: Purify our consciences from works of death
Keep our bodies clean for longer
Make the old tabernacle holy again

cards.text: Christ, through the eternal Spirit, offered Himself unblemished to God. Friend, He brought HIMSELF.

cards.question: Christ's blood purifies our consciences so that we may serve the living God.

findings.problem: Hebrews 9:2-5 is a list of the tabernacle's rooms and furnishings. Not much happens in it, and the writer himself says 'we cannot discuss these things in detail now.' The walkthrough spreads it over cards 2 to 7 and gives it a choice card about one item in the ark (Aaron's staff). That card tests a detail and doesn't move the passage forward. The two-room layout matters to the argument and can be told, but the furnishings should be summed up on one story card, with a standout detail if it helps.

rule.text: Papa Dorin sums up the stretch in one story card. ... He says in a few words what it covers and doesn't go item by item. He can name a standout detail the text gives if it helps the stretch stick. The baker should know the stretch is there and what it's about, not memorize it. A long stretch never gets a choice card.

findings.problem: Too many choice cards in stop 1 can't be reasoned out and depend on luck. Card 3 (the room's name), card 5 (what's in the ark), card 11 (never without blood) and card 12 (offered for himself) all come with no setup that points the baker to the answer. Cards 11 and 12 run back to back on 9:7 with no story card giving context. That's 4 of the stop's 9 choice cards, so the stop goes past 'a few' discovery questions.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer. The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question. A few discovery questions are fine. Some moments can't be reasoned out, like where Jonah's ship is headed. A few of those are okay, as long as most choice cards are informed guesses.

findings.problem: The right answer, 'Purify our consciences from works of death,' uses the passage's own wording and sounds much more like the Bible than the plain wrong answers 'Keep our bodies clean for longer' and 'Make the old tabernacle holy again.' A baker could pick it for its style alone.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.
